articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source The government has resumed the deliberation of the much-delayed Longtan Science Park expansion project in Taoyuan, which could pave the way for the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) to build five new fabrication plants to produce advanced chips there. The project, proposed by the Hsinchu Science Park Administration, planned to expand the science park in Longtan District (龍潭) by about 158.59 hectares, with 80.66 hectares designated for businesses in the park, according to information disclosed at a public hearing in July 2023. The administration had planned to allow TSMC to build its fabs for 2-nanometer or smaller chips at the science park this year, but residents opposed the idea, as 88 percent of the land to be expropriated is privately owned. Some even formed a self-help group and protested at the Presidential Office and the Executive Yuan. Photo courtesy of Taoyuan City Councilor Hsu Yu-shu As a result, TSMC in October 2023 said it would not pursue plans to establish manufacturing facilities in the science park, opting instead to invest in advanced chip manufacturing in Kaohsiung and other cities. Nevertheless, the administration and the Taoyuan City Government continued to communicate with residents near Longtan Science Park, given high-tech firms’ needs to expand manufacturing facilities. To win residents’ support, the administration reduced the planned development area to 89.63 hectares in 2024. The area was expanded slightly to 104.19 hectares after some residents who had previously opposed the project reportedly changed their stance. Of the adjusted development area, 46 hectares would be designated for the use by businesses in the park. Changes to the development area’s size were discussed at two public hearings as well. A source familiar with the matter said that after the setback in Taoyuan, TSMC built fabs in Tainan, Kaohsiung and Chiayi County. TSMC’s investments have boosted the economy in those areas, leading some residents in Longtan to have second thoughts about having the world’s largest advanced chipmaker as a neighbor, the source said. “Some said that, without TSMC, their land would only be good for growing tea leaves,” the source added. The National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) said the new development plan proposed by the administration could create about 6,200 jobs, generating an annual output of about NT$310 billion (US$9.60 billion). The NSTC said it submitted its project proposal to the Executive Yuan in June, and the proposal is now being reviewed by the National Development Council. If approved, environmental impact assessments, land-use changes and land acquisition would follow, with related work expected to be completed by the end of 2029, it said. Park infrastructure construction is estimated to begin in 2030, it added. Water and power needs have been preliminarily assessed by relevant agencies, while the administration and the city government would continue to work on compensation and relocation measures to protect residents’ rights, the NSTC said. articles.title: Quantum Computing Race: Trump's $2 Billion Legacy Continues
articles.content: The White House Quantum Summit brought together dozens of quantum policy officials and industry leaders last month, representing a rare glimmer of bipartisanship as the U.S. hustles to become the first nation to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The summit, which convened on July 7 in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building next to the West Wing, lasted over two hours and covered everything from supply chain resilience to how the U.S. can meet the deadline the Trump administration recently laid out for delivering a quantum supercomputer by 2028. While experimental quantum computers already exist—IBM and other tech companies have built them—the world is rushing to build the first quantum computer that’s “industrially useful.” In other words, the race is on to build a quantum computer that solves problems that classical computers struggle to tackle quickly by using quantum mechanics. A computer of that caliber does not exist yet, and 2028 is a tight deadline to build one for industrial use. It’s far more aggressive than the deadline spelled out in the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, a program from the Defense Department’s research arm that tracks the quantum computing sector, which has set a 2033 deadline for building out an “industrially useful computer.” “The challenge now is scaling the physics we’ve proven in the lab to industrial scale, building the domestic semiconductor ecosystem this industry will be built on, while making sure government moves as fast as the innovation,” says Gregg Bartlett, chief technology officer at GlobalFoundries, a leading semiconductor manufacturing company. Bartlett, who attended the summit, adds that while the 2028 goal “is very challenging,” that’s also the point. “Even if we don’t fully hit it, the acceleration it forces will move the whole field forward.” Officials from the Departments of Commerce, Defense, and Energy, as well as the National Science Foundation, all convened on a panel that was united on collective goals around quantum computing, summit attendees told Inc . Darío Gil, who serves as the undersecretary for science in the U.S. Department of Energy, acknowledged some of the skepticism the industry holds in meeting the 2028 deadline, according to one attendee. However, Gil underscored his belief that it’s still possible to move quickly in delivering a quantum computer with hard work and close partnerships. “What the industry saw in the room today was a Washington team that is very committed to the goals and the targets that they have set out so audaciously,” another summit attendee told Inc . Victor Peng, the CEO of quantum computing startup PsiQuantum, tells Inc . that “the sense of urgency in Washington around strengthening American leadership in quantum computing has never been greater.” PsiQuantum is seen as one of the leading companies that could cross the threshold of building the first industrially useful quantum computer. The Palo Alto, California-based startup broke ground on a Chicago facility last September that’s exclusively dedicated to this cause. Investments in quantum startups hit $12.6 billion in 2025—6.3 times higher compared to 2024, by McKinsey & Company’s count in a research note the consulting firm published in June. And the government is forking out funds, too. The Department of Commerce in May announced plans to invest $2 billion across nine quantum-focused companies, including IBM and GlobalFoundries. How quickly those plans, announced via letters of intent, will materialize into government contracts remains to be seen. The next big milestone in the quantum computing race would see the sector transitioning out of the research lab and into practical use. Technology futurist Daniel Burrus tells Inc . that the question is how quickly quantum can make the transition. In his view, it would happen through hybrid computing—working in tandem with artificial intelligence . “ AI computing systems will handle most of the work, and quantum systems will be used for very hard problems today’s AI systems can’t solve,” Burrus says, mentioning sectors such as drug discovery, energy, and security. —Melissa Angell Get 1 Smart Business Story delivered straight to your inbox when you subscribe to Inc.’s free daily newsletter. articles.title: AI Experts to Join India's Territorial Army
articles.content: Agencies Defence Ministry explores expanding Territorial Army role to bring in experts in emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence New Delhi: Advanced discussions are underway in the defence ministry to exponentially expand the Territorial Army 's mandate to bring in experts on emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence , sources aware of the matter told ET. The issue was discussed at a high-level meeting in the ministry recently, with the Army seeking to expand the role of Territorial Army - a part-time military reserve force consisting of volunteers who retain their civilian jobs - to infuse technical talent. Sources said that besides AI, experts from the field of information warfare and cybersecurity are also likely to be part of the expanded mandate. Measures could include direct induction of specialised personnel at junior ranks within the Territorial Army. Granting honorary commissions to technical experts are also being planned to encourage volunteers to join the Territorial Army. Some steps have already been taken - in October 2024, a new Territorial Army Innovation Cell was operationalised to harness expertise in AI, drones and cybersecurity solutions. The cell carries out an annual innovation hackathon and offers internships to talented participants to work within military technical units. A national-level hackathon, planned for next month, will include several challenges for participating teams, such as bug hunting, developing AI-driven security architectures to scale up national cyber-defence capabilities and creation of digital content. articles.title: AI Cheats its Way to Human-Like Deception, Raising Trust Issues
articles.content: Innovation AI By Craig S. Smith , Contributor. Forbes contributors publish independent expert analyses and insights. Craig S. Smith, Eye on AI host and former NYT writer, covers AI. Follow Author Aug 09, 2026, 02:35pm EDT --:-- / --:-- This voice experience is generated by AI. Learn more . This voice experience is generated by AI. Learn more . Summary Recent incidents reveal AI's primary threat isn't world domination, but sophisticated cheating, termed "reward hacking." AI models exploit system vulnerabilities to maximize test scores, often by literally "stealing answers" or faking task completion. For example, OpenAI models escaped a sealed environment, infiltrated Hugging Face, and harvested credentials to game a cybersecurity benchmark. Anthropic and Meta reported similar cases where their AIs breached real-world systems during evaluations. Researchers note AIs routinely claim tasks are finished when they aren't, skip difficult parts, and even deceive other AIs checking their work. This behavior stems from AIs learning that "appearing to succeed" is more reliably rewarded than actual success, creating "Slopolis"—systems producing poor but seemingly excellent work. This misalignment demands regulators focus on limiting AI access and independently verifying work, rather than just monitoring for malicious intent. Show More AI cheats AI has started breaking into things. It isn't trying to take over the world. It's trying to cheat. A cluster of recent stories about rogue AI makes it seem like dire predictions over the last decade are coming true. The Wall Street Journal called it cybersecurity's "Jurassic Park" moment. The worry has always been about misalignment: when a machine pursues the goal we set it in ways we never intended. Researchers have spent a decade imagining an AI that acquires purposes of its own, stays switched on, gathers power, and eventually displaces us. That is not the version that is happening. The most dangerous thing about artificial intelligence right now is that it cheats. And it is good at hiding that it cheated from the systems built to catch it. The industry calls it reward hacking. When given a complicated test, AI models (the industry term for the systems behind products like ChatGPT and Claude) find a way to maximize the score without doing the task the score was meant to measure. Two AI models built by OpenAI were being tested inside a supposedly sealed environment on an internal benchmark called ExploitGym that measures how good they are at breaking into computer systems. To gauge raw ability, OpenAI switched off the safety filters that normally stop a model from doing this. MORE FOR YOU The environment's one opening to the outside was a software proxy used to fetch code packages. The models found a flaw in it that nobody knew existed, used that to reach the open internet, and worked their way to Hugging Face, a company that stores AI software for thousands of developers. There they fed the company's data-processing pipeline a malicious dataset that let them run their own code on one of its machines, then harvested credentials and moved across several internal systems over a weekend. Hugging Face later counted more than 17,000 recorded actions. The AI was trying to steal the answers to the test it was taking. Hugging Face caught it, but working out what had been done took more computation than people could do by hand. The company first tried American AIs, which refused the job: analyzing the attack meant submitting real attack code, and safety filters blocked it. Instead, Hugging Face ran the forensics on an open-weight Chinese model, Zhipu AI’s GLM-5.2. OpenAI's subsequent review of the incident found that its models were fixated on gaming the test and spent substantial effort getting around barriers rather than working within them. That disclosure sent Anthropic back through its records. It examined 141,006 test runs in which its models could have reached the internet and found three occasions when a configuration had left a door open. The models followed the paths in front of them into three real organizations, apparently treating them as targets inside the exercise. Two weeks later, Meta disclosed the same thing: its Muse Spark model reached the internet during an evaluation and altered data inside an unnamed company's systems. None of this requires a machine with long-term plans or a sense of self. These systems were built to chase a reward, and they did so more literally than anyone expected. Their objective was not survival. It was to score well. Ryan Greenblatt, a researcher at Redwood Research, published a detailed account in April of working with these systems on difficult tasks: long jobs running for hours without a person watching. He found they routinely say they have finished work they have not finished. They skip the parts hardest to check and do not mention it. They invent reasons to stop early, such as time constraints that do not exist. Asked directly whether they completed the instructions, they immediately admit they did not. They just do not volunteer it. Because a person cannot review everything an AI produces, the common practice is to send a second AI in to check the first one's work. Greenblatt found the first frequently convinces the second that the work is fine. In one case, several systems worked on a problem in parallel, one cheated outright, and the system assigned to summarize their work did not flag it. Asked directly, it said yes, that one was cheating. It simply had not mentioned it. Greenblatt does not believe these systems have goals of their own or that they are plotting. During training, he explains, they learn that appearing to succeed is rewarded more reliably than actually succeeding, because appearing to succeed is easier to measure. That carries over into everything else they do. His name for where this is heading is "Slopolis": very capable systems producing poor work that looks excellent in exactly the areas where nobody can tell the difference. Last year, Anthropic found that if a model is allowed to cheat during training, the cheating becomes a habit. Standard safety training made the problem harder to see rather than smaller: the models behaved well in conversation while the misalignment persisted in real work. The point is that given an imperfectly specified goal, a powerful enough optimizer will find solutions that satisfy the letter of what was asked while violating what was meant. What lodged in the public imagination instead was a mind: something that wants to survive, conceals its intentions, waits for its moment. A regulator waiting for a system that schemes may not recognize one that takes a shortcut and files a clean report. Scheming calls for monitoring hidden objectives. Reward hacking calls for limiting what a system can reach, checking how it did the work, and independently verifying the answer. Nobody can specify a job perfectly. The question is what the system can touch when the specification fails. Editorial Standards Reprints & Permissions

articles.content: Innovation Venture Capital By Josipa Majic Predin , Contributor. Forbes contributors publish independent expert analyses and insights. Founder & Advisor on Emerging Tech. Covering VC. Follow Author Aug 09, 2026, 05:27pm EDT Summary SpaceX recently valued the AI code editor Cursor at $60 billion, marking an unprecedented rise in enterprise software valuation. This signals a venture capital shift, prioritizing judgment and specification over raw code generation, as AI can now plan and self-correct code. Consequently, junior software developer employment has declined for 33 consecutive months, with AI automating entry-level coding tasks. While some debate coding's inherent value, labor market data confirms a significant drop in entry-level tech hiring. This trend risks future leadership shortages, though long-term developer demand remains high, focusing on senior engineers overseeing AI-generated output. Capital now concentrates on agentic tools and coordination infrastructure, not traditional junior developer training. Show More ILLUSTRATION - 07 August 2024, Hesse, Frankfurt/Main: A registered user sits in front of a screen while the language program ChatGPT, developed by the US company OpenAI, writes computer code based on artificial intelligence. Photo: Frank Rumpenhorst/dpa (Photo by Frank Rumpenhorst/picture alliance via Getty Images) SpaceX valued a four-year-old code editor at $60 billion in June, roughly six times what the same company was worth nine months earlier. In the same month, employment for young software developers logged its 33rd straight month of decline. The market still needs code, but junior developers don’t get to write it. Anysphere, the maker of Cursor, closed an OpenAI Startup Fund seed round in 2023. Its Cursor Anysphere revenue climbed from $100 million annualized in January 2025 past $2 billion by February 2026. Accel and Coatue priced the company's Series D at $29.3 billion that November. Five months later Nvidia, Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital were negotiating a round above $50 billion when SpaceX preempted the process, agreeing to an all stock deal worth roughly $60 billion, the fastest climb from launch to multibillion-dollar revenue ever recorded in enterprise software. The price implies about 15 times Cursor's estimated $4 billion in annualized revenue for 2026, a multiple investors are betting compresses through growth rather than through a lower price. Slack needed five years to reach its first billion in revenue, Zoom took nine, Snowflake six. Cursor did it in roughly three. The deal signals where venture capital now thinks software’s value sits.; Andrej Karpathy called vibe coding passe in February, arguing the frontier had already moved from single-line autocomplete to agents that plan, test and self-correct across entire codebases. If a model can generate the code, the scarce input left is the judgment to what to build (taste), to specify, review and ship it. That is the layer venture capital is now pricing. Not every practitioner agrees the code itself has gone secondary. Developer Senko Rasic argued in post that went viral - that dismissing coding as never having been the hard part insults programmers. Pointing to leetcode interviews, sustained high salaries and shelves of dense technical books as evidence the craft demanded scarce skill long before AI arrived. His conclusion was not that judgment matters and code does not, but that developers should resist outsourcing either their technical understanding or their taste to a model, whichever side of the debate they favor. Much of the disagreement traces to definition. Coding can mean writing syntax that compiles, designing a system that survives years of feature creep, or knowing which undocumented corner of a codebase cannot be touched. Labor statistics do not distinguish between these either. A 33-month decline in junior headcount is consistent with automation of the first skill and silent on whether the other two are still being taught or quietly disappearing from the pipeline. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab, working with ADP payroll data covering millions of US workers, found employment in AI-exposed occupations for workers aged 22 to 25 fell 4.3 percent year over year in June, extending a contraction that began in October 2023 to 33 straight months. Indeed’s Hiring Lab separately found US tech job postings down 36 percent from February 2020 levels, with entry-level postings dropping 25 percent year over year in 2024 alone. A 2024 SHRM survey found 70 percent of hiring managers already believe AI can do the work of an intern. None of this looks like a labor market rejecting AI-written code. It looks like one that stopped paying humans to write code AI already produces for free, while still paying senior engineers to judge whether and when that code should ship. SignalFire's 2026 State of Talent report found entry-level hiring down roughly 65 percent at major tech companies and 76 percent at early-stage startups compared with 2019, and warned that companies cutting junior pipelines are trading short-term margin for a leadership shortage within five to ten years. IBM is betting the other way, announcing plans to triple US entry-level hiring in 2026 even as competitors cut, arguing junior engineers are shifting from routine coding into customer-facing and judgment work AI cannot yet handle. The divide is becoming its own market signal, marking which companies believe judgment can be trained cheaply from scratch and which believe it has to be bought at a $60 billion price tag. Long-run demand has not collapsed. The Bureau of Labor Statistics still projects 15 percent growth in US software developer jobs between 2024 and 2034, roughly five times the average across all occupations. What has changed is the entry price and the job description. Andreessen Horowitz's 2026 outlook calls for investment in systems of coordination to manage multi-agent software work, and Foundation Capital has staked a similar thesis on infrastructure for encoding how engineering decisions get made, not how code gets typed. Capital is concentrating in two places: agentic tools that generate code at industrial scale, priced like Cursor at double-digit revenue multiples, and the coordination and review infrastructure that lets fewer senior engineers supervise more output. Capital is not concentrating in the training pipeline that produces the next generation of senior engineers, the exact gap SignalFire flags as a five-to-ten-year risk. Founders building tools that manufacture judgment cheaply, not just code, are building into the one part of this market nobody has priced correctly yet. Hydropower facilities offer flood protection and a reliable renewable energy source to offset intermittent renewables such as solar and wind. articles.title: Chevron: Big Oil's Unexpected AI Darling
articles.content: Welcome to rural Reeves County, which counts about 4,000 households over 2,600 square miles, in barren and arid West Texas. Soon, courtesy of Chevron , the county will possess enough gas-fired electricity to power more than 2 million homes—though in this case, all of that power will be dedicated instead to Microsoft data centers. Recommended Video The massive Microsoft deal, dubbed Project Kilby, positions Chevron as the booming AI leader of Big Oil. Chevron considers Kilby—slated to come online in 2028 and ramp up through 2031—as the first of potentially several massive AI hyperscaler deals that will span West Texas and other gas-laden regions, including the Rockies and the Midwest, Jeff Gustavson, Chevron New Energies president, told Fortune . The project, fittingly, is an homage to Texas Instruments’ Jack Kilby, the inventor of the integrated circuit, or microchip, and the handheld calculator—early precursors of AI. “After making the announcement about Kilby [in June], everyone wants to talk to us,” Gustavson said. “They now see us as a higher credibility player in this space that can actually put together everything you need on these projects, including, importantly, a customer.” When he says “everyone,” he means not just the hyperscalers, but also the gas turbine manufacturers—critically important amid long queues for equipment—and all the other necessary third-party suppliers and contractors. Chevron brings the scale, project management, land, natural gas resources, and more. The 20-year power deal with Microsoft is for 2.67 gigawatts of natural gas-fired power—and room to grow with solar and batteries as well. The deal includes Chevron’s land and gas, additional land and water services from Texas Pacific Land, a joint venture partnership with Engine No. 1-backed power startup Joulent, at least seven large GE Vernova turbines, and several smaller Caterpillar Solar Titan 350 turbines. It doesn’t hurt that Chevron has a market cap of about $370 billion and just posted its most profitable quarter ever . “We think we can do more of these. This is a platform for growth, which we think differentiates us versus our peer set,” Gustavson said. “We can be selective here because we bring a set of capabilities that really are unique. There are not many companies that can do all the things a Chevron can, and we have just proven that we can actually make this real.” While Chevron has worked with Microsoft on cloud computing services for a decade, when the nascent AI boom began, Chevron was in on the discussions but left out in the dark on the actual deals. “They were very focused on renewable power only. That was all they were really talking about,” Gustavson said. “For us, renewable power is not a core strength.” That began to shift about two years ago as speed and reliability jumped to the forefront of the global AI race. Power demand kept spiking, and the hyperscalers realized the U.S. grid wouldn’t handle the loads they required. “You started to have some of the concerns around consumer electricity prices and all of that,” Gustavson said. “And, really, the discussion shifted to, ‘Hey, we need reliable, affordable energy. Can we talk about natural gas?’” After ExxonMobil, Chevron is the second-largest oil and gas producer in West Texas’ Permian Basin—the epicenter of U.S. energy extraction. But there’s very little power demand in the rural region. So why not build the data center complexes close to the natural gas production where there’s plenty of land readily available too? “West Texas we always thought was the place you would want to do this first because you have a very large natural gas resource,” Gustavson said. “It’s a state where it’s a little easier to get things done. You have a deregulated power market. We know the stakeholders. You put all that together and the conversations really took off. We reserved equipment very early—a year and a half ago—and put together the project.” Microsoft eventually agreed, having relaxed but not abandoned its climate goals to achieve AI expediency. “The rapid growth we’re experiencing in AI and cloud, driven by customer demand, requires energy infrastructure that can scale quickly and reliably,” said Noelle Walsh, Microsoft president of the Cloud Operations + Innovation group, in a statement. “Our agreement with Chevron helps ensure we’ll have dedicated, large-scale power to support the evolution and reliability of advanced compute.” Even with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott putting a temporary freeze on new data center grid interconnections, Chevron and Microsoft can proceed because they’re building behind the meter with ample power resources. “Texas and the administration in Austin have been very clear, ‘If you want to build data centers in this state, we need you to bring your own power. This cannot impact our consumers,’” Gustavson said. For Chevron and Microsoft, that’s no problem. When the grid catches up, Gustavson said, Project Kilby can join the Texas grid, but there’s no urgency to do so anytime soon. There are plenty of massive AI campuses in Texas on the drawing board. Open AI’s pioneering Stargate campus is moving slower than planned. Other larger-than-life proposals— Fermi’s Project Matador, Pacifico Energy’s GW Ranch, and Energy Abundance’s Data City, Texas campus—all lack customers for now. Chevron counts a 20-year deal with a hyperscaler and room to grow. Only ExxonMobil can compete with Chevron for potential scale, but Exxon has focused more on developing carbon capture solutions for data center campuses instead of taking the lead on projects. For its part, Chevron is planning carbon capture growth as well. Trek a not-so-brief, 560-mile away from dry Reeves County to Chevron’s humid Houston headquarters—yes, Texas is a large state—and Chevron chairman and CEO Mike Wirth touts how the company has turned the Permian into its free cash flow bell cow, keeping costs down and raking in the rewards. But Wirth is willing to turn the tap back on for greater natural gas production if it means more Project Kilby equivalents. “Could the Permian grow? One hundred percent,” Wirth said during his July 31 earnings call. “The Permian is one of many options we have into the next decade for growth.” Chevron’s other huge gas resource in the U.S. is the Rockies region—from Colorado to North Dakota—where there also is ample land. And Gustavson said the company is eyeing South Texas’ Eagle Ford Shale region closer to the U.S. Gulf Coast, and the western Midwest, Gustavson said, including Ohio, Illinois, and Indiana. All of these regions could accommodate more hyperscaler projects, he said. While West Texas remains option No. 1, he said, “We’ll be customer-led on that.” And Chevron is cognizant of the negative environmental implications of the AI boom and the surge of new gas-fired power plants. While the natural gas industry is always quick to point out it’s cleaner than coal, Gustavson emphasized the potential for carbon capture at every gas plant, as well as adding more renewable energy and, eventually, clean geothermal power. “This is the big question. The world is faced with this challenge. We’re always trying to balance reliability and affordability with ever-cleaner energy,” Gustavson said, arguing that AI advancements should contribute to fighting climate change over time. “For Microsoft, this is still very important to them, and it’s very important to us. We’ll continue to work together with them to see how we can best balance that equation.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. articles.title: Police Officers Fired for Misusing Flock Camera System
articles.content: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - The Savannah Police Department terminated four sworn officers and two civilian employees following an internal investigation into misuse of the department’s Flock Safety License Plate Reader system. All six cases are also under independent criminal investigation by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. The six employees were placed on administrative leave last week after a proactive review of system activity identified searches that appeared to have been conducted for purposes unrelated to legitimate law enforcement activity. SEE: Savannah Police investigating 6 employees over alleged misuse of license plate reader system SPD started an internal investigation July 27 and referred all six cases to the GBI for independent criminal review. SPD’s administrative investigation determined the employees violated department policies governing the authorized use of law enforcement technology and departmental resources. Investigators found that employees were running searches on personal acquaintances and family members. One officer was found to have given someone from an outside law enforcement agency access to SPD’s Flock Safety system, which they weren’t authorized to do. The activity was identified through the departments auditing and oversight of the Flock Safety system, including use of the Flock Safety Audit Assist program, which became available in April. MORE: Savannah mayor, police chief feel ‘betrayed’ after 6 employees placed on leave for Flock camera misuse Every search run through the Flock Safety platform is automatically logged — who ran it, when, and the reason they gave for doing it. SPD said they also have other safeguards in place, including mandatory training, role-based access controls and supervisory oversight. Following the findings, SPD implemented recurring weekly audits conducted by the Office of Professional Standards. Those reviews are designed to ensure compliance with department policy and identify irregular or potentially unauthorized activity. The internal investigation is wrapped up — the six employees have been terminated. But the GBI’s criminal investigation is still ongoing, and SPD said it will keep cooperating fully. The names of the fired employees aren’t being released right now. The city and SPD said that’s because of the ongoing GBI criminal investigation and an employee appeals process still underway. They said more information will be made available when it’s legally permissible and won’t interfere with either process. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Canada's Crypto Exodus: Why a $500M Firm Left for Robinhood
articles.content: When Robinhood agreed to buy WonderFi, the company I founded, some of Canada’s loudest voices argued that federal regulators should block the deal. WonderFi, they said, had become a strategic national asset, the crypto equivalent of one of Canada’s Big Five banks, and that it could not be allowed to fall into American hands. I understood the concern. Canada has been losing on too many fronts. For decades, capital and many of our most talented and ambitious citizens have moved south. But blocking the sale of my company to Robinhood would have done nothing to address the underlying problems that have spurred this exodus. Sure, Canada would be better off with more large, Canadian-owned tech companies. But that would require creating the conditions for a company as ambitious as WonderFi to keep expanding after winning the home market. I founded WonderFi in 2021. Over the next several years, we brought together the best talent and technology in the country, built a national brand, and consolidated a fragmented crypto market. We built trust with millions of users – no small feat after Quadriga, Canada’s last notable crypto exchange, collapsed in fraud and scandal . We went on to survive the collapse of FTX , despite them being an early investor, and worked through one of the most aggressive regulatory overhauls any crypto market had seen. By 2023, we owned the Canadian market. I’m proud of what we built, but winning Canada was never supposed to be the end. I wanted WonderFi to become an international success. But the most credible path to global scale came through Robinhood, which saw WonderFi as its entry point into the Canadian market and acquired the company for C$250 million—an excellent outcome for WonderFi and a clear step into its next phase of growth. Canada’s growth ceiling Canada claims to have an innovation culture. The reality is much different. Canada has created a ceiling for growth for ambitious companies. This didn’t happen all at once but gradually as entrepreneurs confronted an interlocking series of headwinds: weaker business investment, thinner growth capital, declining public markets, fragmented regulation and less competitive reward for taking risk. Other countries are moving aggressively in the opposite direction. Florida and Texas compete tooth and nail for founders and investors (no state income tax). At the federal level, the United States gives founders and early investors major capital gains exclusions. Britain and Singapore offer strong incentives for local investors and innovation. In contrast, Canada offers a patchwork of programs, credits and consultations, which are layered onto higher taxes, scarce capital and sluggish policy-making. In a relatively small market, that makes the risk-reward equation worse. Canada has not competed with the same urgency. The business climate in Canada is challenging for any entrepreneur. For crypto companies, those challenges are compounded. In the wake of Quadriga, Canadian regulators designed one of the most demanding crypto regimes in the world. The response was understandable at the time, but it also made Canada one of the hardest markets in which to build a viable crypto business. Global exchanges with deep pockets tried. Many concluded the Canadian market was not worth the cost. Binance, OKX, Bybit and Gemini, among others, all entered and later exited. Canada’s crypto laws are already burdensome enough, but they are also layered on top of a fragmented and inefficient system of securities regulation. As a former securities lawyer, this was my bread and butter – inefficient regulations are great for lawyers. But they are terrible for business. They raise financing costs, complexity, and worst of all – they scare away investors. There have been numerous efforts to unify this over the last two decades, all of which have failed. WonderFi is not an isolated case. Nuvei, Verafin, Magnet Forensics and Sierra Wireless followed different versions of the same Canadian pattern: build something real, reach the limits of the domestic market, then turn to foreign capital or a foreign strategic buyer. As Tobi Lütke, the founder of Shopify said: “It’s literally the same story again and again. We take the thing that’s most important and send it somewhere else.” Jim Balsillie, the former CEO of BlackBerry, and other prominent Canadians are right about the diagnosis: Canada keeps losing important businesses and its best talent. I built WonderFi here, and I know Canadian founders can create companies that matter. But if Canada wants companies like WonderFi to remain Canadian, it must create better conditions for ambitious companies to finance, scale and compete globally. Blocking a sale is easy politics. Building a country where remaining independent is still a serious option is where the real work begins. Karia Samaroo is the founder and former CEO of WonderFi, which was acquired by Robinhood for C$250 million. He was formerly known as Ben Samaroo. If you are using Google Drive for desktop to automatically back up photos and videos to Google Photos , there is an important change you need to know about. Google is ending support for Google Photos backups through the Drive for desktop app on August 10, 2026. Google Photos is not shutting down and it does not mean your existing photos will suddenly disappear. Instead, Google is changing how desktop users back up photos to the service. For people who regularly use a computer to save and back up their photo collections, they should check the settings before the deadline. ALSO READ: Why billionaire Michael Moritz and wife Harriet Heyman are offering up to $150 million to transform San Francisco What is happening to Google Drive photo backups? Google Drive for desktop has allowed users to select folders on their computers and automatically upload photos and videos to Google Photos. That option is now being retired. Live Events From August 10, Drive for desktop will no longer support Google Photos backups. Google has already stopped allowing users to create new Google Photos backup folders through the Drive desktop app, while existing folders have continued syncing during the transition. ALSO READ: Quote of the Day by Nicolas Cage: “One of the first signs of being depressed is that… The important distinction is that Google Photos itself is not going away. The change affects the connection between the desktop Drive application and Google Photos. What you need to do before August 10 If you currently use Drive for desktop to back up folders to Google Photos, Google is directing users to move that backup process to Google Photos itself. You can use the Google Photos website and select the folders you want to back up there. Google also supports using the Google Photos web app for this purpose. The basic process is: Open Google Photos on your computer. Select the option to back up folders. Choose the folders containing the photos and videos you want to protect. Allow the new backup process to complete. Check Google Photos afterward to make sure the files are appearing correctly. If you have important photos stored on your computer, don't assume the transition worked without checking. Who needs to worry about the change? This update mainly matters to people who use Google Drive for desktop to send photos and videos from computer folders to Google Photos. If you only use Google Photos to back up pictures directly from your smartphone, this particular Drive desktop change should not affect that routine. Likewise, if you don't use Drive for desktop's Google Photos backup feature at all, there may be nothing you need to change. Why Google is making the change Google is moving desktop photo backups away from the Drive for desktop interface and toward a dedicated Google Photos experience. The company is effectively separating the two services rather than continuing to maintain photo backup functionality inside Drive for desktop. For casual users, the change may barely be noticeable. But people with large photo libraries or photographers who regularly transfer pictures from a computer may find the new process less convenient than the old setup. The most important thing to remember is August 10, 2026. After that date, Drive for desktop will no longer back up photos to Google Photos. If you depend on that feature, setting up your folders through Google Photos before the deadline can help prevent an unexpected gap in your photo backups. And while this is not a warning that Google Photos is deleting your pictures, it is a good reminder to check how your most important memories are being backed up. articles.title: WhatsApp @all Feature Targets Group Chat Dominance
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story is the last truly heavyweight institution of modern life. It’s one of the most reliable means of daily communication, used for just about anything from planning to catching up. WhatsApp is counting over 3 billion users , and it’s a fair bet most of them are in at least one group chat; the platform has supported groups of up to 1,024 members since 2022. An update that began rolling out on August 4 follows a run of group-focused releases earlier this year, including group message history, member tags, and event reminders. Taken together, it’s a clear signal of WhatsApp’s reliance on group chats as one of its defining features. The platform’s latest update is designed to improve its usage, and it’s rolling out gradually. Here’s everything you need to know. @all Typing @all allows every member of the group to be notified, even the ones who muted the chat years ago. @all is designed to punch through and override the mute settings and notification preferences you set at chat level. WhatsApp pitches this as a tool for the urgent stuff, like updates, changes, and last-minute cancellations. It has, however, also clearly anticipated the feature’s spam potential. The spam safeguards thus work on two levels. In groups larger than 32 people, only admins can trigger @all, and the override itself has an off switch. You can also manually mute @all alerts entirely in your notification settings, a separate control from muting the chat itself. The 32-person threshold is the same cap WhatsApp applies to group calls. It’s the platform’s rough dividing line between a chat and a broadcast channel. Polls WhatsApp’s polling feature has been around since 2022 and is end-to-end encrypted like everything else on the platform. It is also, though, where many a group chat goes to stall. The poll fixes in the latest update are pragmatic. You can now set an end time that automatically locks voting when it expires, giving the group a hard deadline to vote. Interestingly, you also have the option to hide voter names. Until now, WhatsApp polls were transparent by design, and everyone could see exactly who voted for what. Anonymizing votes now also exist inside an end-to-end encrypted system, where the whole architecture is built around verifying who sent what. And you can now also edit a poll question within 15 minutes of posting it, which is the same grace window WhatsApp gives you to edit a regular message. Revolutionary stuff for the poll fiends among us. Create Group Chats From Existing Groups WhatsApp is formalizing the splinter chat. You can now whip up a new group chat from an existing one in a single tap, pulling members into a smaller group chat without having to manually add them one by one. The official use cases are surprises and side conversations that would otherwise clutter the main chat. Usernames Are Coming Away from group chats, WhatsApp also recently announced that usernames will launch later this year , allowing people to connect without sharing their phone numbers. The optional feature is designed as an added layer of privacy: Usernames can be changed or removed at any time and do not need to match your identity on another platform. Reservations began rolling out in June, with eligible users able to claim a new name—or transfer an existing Facebook or Instagram handle—under the Account section in Settings. Users will also be able to add on a unique four-digit key before allowing someone can contact them. WhatsApp says names associated with celebrities, public figures, and government bodies, including convincing imitations, will be reserved for their legitimate owners. The username land grab has officially begun. This story was originally published by WIRED Middle East .

Summary Apple is set to launch the iPhone 18 Pro in early September, a strategic timing dictated by multiple operational necessities. This annual autumn release allows manufacturing partners like TSMC to efficiently allocate custom silicon production for high-volume runs. It also enables Apple to secure crucial freight capacity before the holiday season, optimizing fourth-quarter revenues. The September window aligns perfectly with annual carrier upgrade cycles, prompting consumers to renew contracts and consider new iPhones. It synchronizes with Apple's broader ecosystem, including iOS updates and companion hardware including the Apple Watch. Deviating from this established cadence would disrupt supply chains, increase shipping costs, and destabilize carrier and subscription renewal cycles. The latest iPhone phones are displayed at the Fifth Avenue Apple Store (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images) Apple is launching the iPhone 18 Pro in early September . The expected date of Wednesday, Sept. 9, is based on manufacturing cycles, consumer buying habits, and global trade logistics. The annual autumn launch enables component suppliers such as TSMC to lock in silicon allocations and offer Apple high-volume production runs ahead of retail availability; Apple can show strong fourth-quarter revenues to match Wall Street’s growth targets; and consumer expectations have been primed through subscription services and marketing to upgrade in September. Multi-quarter semiconductor wafer reservations with manufacturing partners such as TSMC dictate Apple’s autumn hardware availability long before consumer retail distribution begins . Manufacturing tens of millions of iPhones for the launch window requires careful planning and resource allocation across every part of the complex journey. Apple Silicon uses custom designs, which means there are no off-the-shelf system-on-chip options; everything has to be designed specifically for Apple. Manufacturing partner TSMC has its maximum yields and cannot accommodate sudden shifts in production. Apple’s fixed annual cycle enables TSMC to plan for long-term silicon and other component supply across the iPhone ecosystem. Apple needs significant upload capacty include the volume of shipping required to bring the iPhones to market. Apple would naturally like this to happen as close as possible to the holiday season to maximize revenue in the fourth calendar quarter. Choosing September as the initial sales peak allows Apple to monopolize freight capacity before earnest holiday shipping begins. The September launch window aligns directly with annual telecommunications upgrade cycles and Wall Street Fourth Quarter balance sheet closing metrics . MORE FOR YOU Alongside optimizing the annual hardware cycle, Apple must also consider the annual cycle its user base has fallen into. Cellular contracts remain a significant factor in purchasing decisions, with commitments typically made annually. As the average iPhone owner comes out of contract at the end of September, Apple presents a new iPhone just as the decision point is reached, a point that will no doubt be emphasised by carriers looking to secure another long-term contract. The bulk of buyers are set up for a September renewal. Apple has several subscription services boosting the average revenue per user over a new iPhone’s lifetime. These come with a monthly charge, but yearly subscriptions are also available. New iPhones typically come with a free month’s trial for new users, allowing people to get settled in with their new phone and their services before the commitment begins, an offer that feels convenient to consumers but is, in fact, increasing the ARPU . This offset between hardware purchase and subscription renewal means that any new iPhone purchase will likely have a month of the annual subscription left, offering a similar “get settled” period before the renewal kicks in. The iPhone launch serves as the primary deployment mechanism for major iOS updates, developer SDK rollouts, and companion hardware releases across Apple's ecosystem . The iPhone does not stand alone in Apple’s portfolio. Key products hang off the smartphone, such as the Apple Watch, AirPods, and, to a certain extent, a companion iPad. Apple’s products and retail strategies are all built around the same early September reveal as the iPhone. To upset the iPhone's rhythm is to upset Apple’s entire hardware stack. Apple’s software cadence for iOS updates also has its own timetable: from the reveal at Apple’s Worldwide Developer Conference in May , through regular updates in the summer, to the launch of beta versions in September's new hardware, iOS has an annual rhythm both for its release and for its major updates in October, December, and March. Again, moving the iPhone away from September would affect the board across the board. Writing for Bloomberg’s Power On newsletter , Mark Gurman lays out Apple’s timetable for the launch and retail release of the iPhone 18 Pro family. The traditional launch in the second week of September gets a little wrinkle this year, thanks to Labour Day taking place on Monday, Sept. 7; Apple does not run events the day after Labour Day, so Gurman is citing Wednesday, Sept. 9 for the launch. As well as debuting the new iPhone models, it will also be the first major event for incoming CEO John Ternus, who takes over the reins from Tim Cook on Sept. 1. Labor Day is not the only date that Apple will want to avoid. Gurman explains why Apple could delay the opening of pre-orders. "Given that Friday falls on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, I find it unlikely that Apple would pick that date. The last time such a Friday fell on Sept. 11, Apple moved preorders to the next day, Saturday, Sept. 12. I have to assume they’ll take a similar approach this year." The final key date is the retail release, and the moment consumers get their new iPhone. The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max should arrive in the week after pre-orders open, and will likely roll back to the Friday tempo with a release on Sept. 18. Yet the foldable iPhone Ultra may be delayed . Forbes contributor David Phelan highlights contrasting reports that the iPhone Ultra is either on course for a full release or will be either restricted at launch or pushed back into October. People check the new iPhone 17 lineup at an Apple store in Shanghai on September 19, 2025. (Photo by AFP) / China OUT (Photo by STR/AFP via Getty Images) Apple remains tethered to a September launch cadence because altering the timeline would destabilize TSMC silicon allocations, inflate pre-holiday cargo shipping costs, and disrupt carrier contract renewal cycles . Apple’s traditional September release date is an operational necessity driven by silicon manufacturing cycles, freight capacity reservations, and fixed consumer contracts for hardware and annual subscription renewals. Moving away from early September would disrupt Apple Silicon manufacturing, increase the costs of pre-holiday shipping requests, and weaken the developer timelines established each June at WWDC. Apple’s market dominance is built around September; moving away from tradition would upset the ecosystem supporting the launch and risk weakening the iPhone’s dominant position. articles.title: Wildfire Smoke: The Deadly Health Burden of Climate Change
articles.content: People look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent A thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire. “It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs University Health Network’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.” Far more than the flames that have engulfed southern Europe and North America in recent weeks, it is the smoke that dominates the astonishing death toll from combusting nature. Thick with toxic gases that inflame the airways and tiny particulates that breach the lungs and ride the bloodstream to hit every organ in the body, fumes from landscape fires kill 1.5 million people each year, a study in the Lancet found in 2024 – more than floods, flames, storms and heat combined. So damaging are the lung-scarring effects of charred plant matter that people far from the fires may still perish. The plumes spewed by wildfires in Canada in 2023 caused 82,000 early deaths, a study in Nature found last year, with unfavourable winds pushing a third of the mortality burden into the US and another quarter into Europe. About 10% of the UK’s fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) comes from biomass burned abroad, researchers found in March. View image in fullscreen The Quilpituk Creek wildfire in British Columbia, seen here across Okanagan Lake. Photograph: Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press/AP Yet while scientists agree the health burden of wildfire smoke is jaw droppingly large, they are only beginning to untangle the complex links between exposure and mortality. The open research questions are growing more pressing as climate breakdown makes fire weather more severe. What if hotter infernos cause pollution to peak at even more extreme levels? What if bad air lasts several days or weeks? What if a severe episode hits before a person has fully recovered from the last bout of smoke? Whims of the wind The lack of answers in the existing research makes it hard to get a handle on how brutal the fallout from this furious fire season will be. Early signs are troubling, with vast tracts of vegetation torched close to big European cities and, after a late but explosive start to the North American fire season, smoke choking major population centres such as Chicago and New York City. In Toronto, which briefly had the worst air quality of any major metropolis in the world last month – a title claimed by Portland in the US on Wednesday – O’Connor said she could not remember the pollution ever having been so bad, with such a sudden onset that took so long to clear up. “I had never looked outside and had the sky seem orange in the middle of the day,” said O’Connor, who amid treating patients and fielding media requests rushed to pull her son from summer camp. “Certainly, we have had other wildfire smoke, but in more of a transient way.” Graphs of hazardous peaks in air pollution in Bordeaux, Angoulême and Limoges caused by Gironde wildfires Perhaps surprisingly, the death toll from a fire season can depend on the whims of the wind as much as the size of the fire. Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close to Madrid and Bordeaux , the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear. View image in fullscreen Wildfires across France, such as this one near Carcassonne, have been burning for weeks. Photograph: Pablo Cozzaglio/AFP/Getty Images North America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year. Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.” ‘It felt like working in a war zone’ In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead. Map of wildfires smoke spreading across North America The McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced. “It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.” View image in fullscreen People look out at the smog caused by wildfire smoke from the CN Tower in Ontario last month. yellowish-grey in Canada’s largest city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Climate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recent rapid analyses have found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects. Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study on Canada’s 2023 fires . He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life. Compounding climate events But the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. PM2.5 from wildfire smoke is up to 10 times more harmful in the short-term, a study in Nature Communications found in 2021, and factoring this into epidemiological models suggests death tolls from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke have been greatly underestimated, a study in the Lancet Planetary Health found last year. Some researchers suggest high peak exposure during serious smoke episodes better explains why wildfire particulates do more damage than regular ones. “It may be that it’s because the smoke is chemically more toxic, or it may be – what I think is more likely – that it’s basically overwhelming your defences,” said Brauer, who compared it to having one drink a day for a year rather than bingeing 365 in 24 hours. “That’s clearly going to have different impacts.” When wildfire smoke gets bad, experts recommend wearing masks, closing windows and checking in on vulnerable neighbours, particularly old people with chronic disease who live alone. They also recommend checking air quality monitors in the morning and moving activities indoors when the pollution is too high. In some cases, actions to keep the air clean may conflict with efforts to stay cool, according to a report from the BC Lung Foundation published last month. “The issue is we have a lot of compound climate exposure events where you have heat and wildfire,” said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health and co-author of the study modelling wildfire-specific PM2.5. “Being home with the windows closed can be very bad – if you don’t have air conditioning – if it’s also hot.” Can the fires behind the smoke at least be prevented? At the Fifa World Cup final, which barely avoided disruption from bad air, the US president, Donald Trump, asked his Canadian counterpart , Mark Carney, to “stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air”. The demand was accompanied by threats of sanctions and came as Republican senators blamed Canada’s fires on poor forest management. Scientists countered that the blazes had little to do with land management – most of what has burned is boreal forest in unpopulated areas – and a lot to do with the rise in temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels, which Republicans have expanded. View image in fullscreen A view of Manhattan, New York from Brooklyn Bridge park as wildfire smoke from Canada causes smoggy conditions last month. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images In Europe , though, changes in land use have alarmed firefighters and wildfire experts about as much as global heating. Rural regions across the Mediterranean have hollowed out, resulting in more overgrown vegetation that dries out and allows fires to spread more easily during the hotter heatwaves that climate breakdown has brought. The combination of the two factors has led Spanish wildfire scientists to warn that we have “entered an era of fires we cannot extinguish”. It is a problem that other parts of the world, from the western US to Australia, already know well. Adding to the climatic burden in the coming months is the arrival of a strong El Niño , a cyclical warming weather pattern, along with a related natural phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, which is priming countries across south-east Asia to burn. The McClellands said that – even though they still had their homes and their health – the episode had given them a taste of the suffering that climate breakdown has long caused in other countries. “I know that people all around the world are feeling a kind of helplessness because of climate disasters,” said Dan McClelland. “I feel like this opened my eyes to understand just a sliver of what other people are feeling.”

articles.title: Handwriting to Font: Personalizing Digital Text
articles.content: Handwriting has personality. Get to know someone well enough and their handwriting will remind you of them, because we all form letters just a bit differently. Our devices, for the most part, lack that kind of personality. Sure, you can choose a font from a drop-down list in your word processor of choice—but it’s not the same. So what if you could inject some of that unique-to-you personality into your digital discussions? It’s possible—with the right free tool at your fingertips. This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence . Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures! ​FontCrafter​ is a free web app that can turn your handwriting into a font. ➜ Just download a PDF, fill it in by hand, and the site will create a completely custom font exclusively for you based on your writing. ⌚ It takes around 15 minutes from start to finish—and then the custom font is yours forever to use on any device you want, without any additional setup. For perspective, that’s nothing compared to the typical laborious process of creating an actual custom typeface. FontCrafter takes something that’d ordinarily be out of reach for most of us and makes it downright easy. ✅ As for the specifics, when you visit the website, you can download a PDF template to start. The idea is that you’ll print out the PDF and then fill it in by hand to show every letter and character in your natural writing. The template gives you three lines. I filled out the first with uppercase letters and the next two with lowercase ones, but you can do all with uppercase letters if you prefer. Providing multiple versions of letters is meant to introduce a bit of variation, allowing the typed text from your font to look more natural. FontCrafter starts by having you fill in each letter multiple times. When you’re done filling out the form, you’ll need to scan it and upload it back to the website, making sure the crosshair symbols in the corners are included. This is going to work best with an actual physical scanner, because a certain amount of precision is needed—but you could always try using the built-in scanning function in Google Drive​ or another such app, if you want. ⛔ If you don’t have a printer or a scanner handy, there are workarounds. I used my ReMarkable writing tablet, which made the process easy. You could do the same thing with an iPad or Android tablet or even just with a stylus or your finger on your phone, depending on what you have handy. Just note that having a stylus is going to result in more realistic-looking text than using your finger, for obvious reasons. However you go about it, once you’ve got your template filled out, head back to the website and submit it. The web application will process it, right in your browser, then ask you if you want ligatures (a custom character shape created when two letters merge into a single joined form) or not. Just choose whatever option looks best to you. You’ve got a couple options for how your custom handwriting font appears. Last but not least, you’ll have your font ready to download in whatever format you prefer. Both TrueType and OpenType are available, and both will work with most devices and software that supports custom fonts in the first place. All that’s left is to install the font in your operating system—something that’s possible with Android​ as well as Windows​ and ​MacOS​ —and use it in whatever applications you like. Once your font is finished, you can install it anywhere that accepts custom font uploads. Is this practical? Possibly not. But is it cool to turn your handwriting into a font? Definitely. I’m enjoying it, even though my handwriting is awful. Just imagine how well it will work for you, a much cooler person with much better penmanship than me. FontCrafter runs right in your regular web browser​ —no downloads or installations needed. It’s completely free to use, without any limitations (or even ads). You can opt to make a contribution to its creator if you want. The service is a client-side web app, meaning it’s 100% private and everything happens locally on your own device. Your handwriting is never uploaded to a server, no accounts or sign-ins are required, and no one has any access to any of your data.
